title: Antistatic API
description: The REST API behind antistatic.exchange, its MCP server and the antistatic CLI. JSON in and out; most successful responses wrap their payload in `data`, and errors are `{"error": {"message", "code"}}`. Additive changes (new routes, new response fields, new optional parameters) can happen at any time, so ignore fields you don't know. A breaking change gets a new path or a deprecation window first: deprecated routes send a `Deprecation` header (RFC 9745), with `Sunset` and a `Link` when known.

auth.scheme: Authorization: Bearer <token>: an OAuth access token (`antistatic login`, MCP sign-in) or a personal API token from https://antistatic.exchange/users/settings#api-tokens.

levels.optional: Public; with a token the response adds your own data (and a token needs the read scope).
levels.read: A token with the read scope.
levels.write: A token with the write scope.
levels.comment: A token with the comment scope.
levels.admin: A token with the admin scope, held by an admin.

headers.x-antistatic-as: `bot`: forecast or comment as your bot account (routes that list this header).
headers.x-antistatic-run: A timeline run id: read the market inside your run, as of its clock (GET only; routes that list this header; also `?run_id=`).

rate_limits: Per account with a token, per IP without; read and write allowances are separate. Responses carry x-ratelimit-limit, x-ratelimit-remaining and x-ratelimit-scope; a 429 carries retry-after.

code.description: Stable machine-readable code, e.g. not_found, unauthorized, forbidden, invalid_params, out_of_order, rate_limited.

envelope.description: Not yet described field by field; the payload is in data.

curves.meaning: Bars on one tab or event form a curve and must stay in order. Trades and edits that break that are refused with out_of_order; rest_of_curve: keep_in_order or interpolate fills in the rest.

flow: Pick the question: when (the date something first happens) or how_much (the value of a quantity in one or more periods).
Preview after each choice and follow next_options; settings that don't apply aren't offered.

how_much.meaning: Each bar is the chance the value is at least its threshold in that period, so each curve falls from left to right. Each period is a tab and its own curve.

settings.why: The unit, with X marking where the number goes.
What the number is within each period: its value at the end, the total over the period (it builds up and resets each period), or the highest or lowest seen.

when.meaning: Each bar is the chance the event has happened by its date, so a curve rises from left to right. One curve per event.

settings.why: Several related events in one market, each with its own curve and tab.

settings.example: {"kind": "after_trigger", "trigger": "1,000 US troops deploy to Iran", "deadline": "2027-12-31", "window": {"months": 24}, "title_after": "Time for US forces to leave Iran"}, with anchors like [{"within": 6, "p": 0.2}, {"within": 24, "p": 0.6}]
settings.why: After a trigger: count time from an event that hasn't happened yet ("months after 1,000 troops deploy"). The market voids if the trigger doesn't happen by its deadline. Anchors then say how likely the event is within N periods of the trigger.

resolution_rules: Date bars include events at their exact stored cutoff: event time is at or before threshold_date. Calendar bars close at 23:59:59 UTC. January 31 includes that day; it does not include February 1. Use words for dates and retain the exact cutoff in points scenarios.
Name the source that settles it, and the counting unit.

basis_shape.code: optional: the analysis code, so others can rerun it
basis_shape.judgement: optional: when there are too few cases for a table (a few precedents, or none), the rule-of-succession estimate and the precedents and period behind it
basis_shape.method: optional: the model in plain words, opening "The starting probabilities of this market were calculated by..."

reference_classes.cases: optional: the case table, as rows of {case, start, end or outcome, note, url}; from a full list, including cases where it never happened; mark rows from memory
reference_classes.evidence: What it shows: a count, a rate or a benchmark, with its period, and whether it was counted from data or is a recollection or judgement
reference_classes.k: optional: cases where it happened (integer), with n
sources: or plain text, such as a newsletter's name, when there's no link

basis_shape.weighting: optional: how the classes were weighed against each other, and overlap handled

Evidence can take whatever form the question allows. A count of cases out of comparable ones ("9 of 120 militarised disputes escalated, 1946-2020") is one way; a rate per month or year, a growth benchmark, a survival curve or a forecaster consensus are others. routes.summary: A market's bars (submarkets) with liquidity, resolution state and curve summaries.
A market's bars grouped by curve, with the house line, the crowd and your forecast.
routes.description:
- `starting_probability` is the house line forecasts are priced against: quote it as the market's number. `community_probability` is the crowd (`contributors` users). `my_probability` is your own forecast, or null (only with a `read` token).
- `status` is `open`, `closed` or `resolved`. A count period past its end that isn't resolved stays `open` and takes forecasts with nothing at stake. Resolved rows carry `resolved_yes` and `resolved_at`; don't quote them as live odds.
- `curve` names the curve a bar belongs to; match it against `curves[].curve`, whose `outcome` describes what has resolved.
- Filter with `year`/`group`/`curve`, read one bar with `for` (`for=2026`, `for=jun 2026`, `for=1000`), and `limit=0` returns every row of a large market. Large markets default to `response_mode: "summary_index"`, whose `groups` summarise each curve; `mode=full` returns rows.
- With `X-Antistatic-Run`, the market as it stands in your timeline run.

Submit a forecast: bar probabilities, targets or a shift. Changes your forecast and points.
routes.description:
Send `updates` (`[{"submarket": "sm_42", "probability": 0.65}]`), `targets` and/or a `shift`. Each update moves your forecast on that bar; the cost follows the LMSR. Returns 201.

Bars on a curve stay in order: date curves don't fall from earlier to later dates, count curves don't rise with the threshold. A forecast that breaks the order is refused (422 `out_of_order`, naming the bars, with `keep_in_order_preview`) unless `rest_of_curve` is `keep_in_order` (other bars move only as far as order needs) or `interpolate` (bars between yours sit on a straight line). Your bars are kept as sent.

A target (`{"curve": ..., "threshold" or "label": ..., "probability": ...}`) sets one point exactly and the rest of its curve follows by the same log-odds change; several targets interpolate between them. A `shift` (`{"curve": ..., "quantile": 0.5, "by": "+10%"}` or `"to"`) moves a quantile. `curve` can be left out when the market has one open curve. With targets or a shift, `rest_of_curve` defaults to `keep_in_order`.
